title: Lost Devotional Letter
subject: Criminal Law & Procedure
stem:
Lydia, a skilled calligrapher, crafted a devotional letter on very old paper. Lydia included details that would lead knowledgeable collectors to believe that the letter had been written decades earlier by Peter, a well-known retired Bible teacher, to his friend Timothy. Lydia had a facsimile of Peter’s autograph, and she made the signature and other writing on the letter resemble Peter’s.

Lydia knew that the letter would attract the attention of collectors of Christian memorabilia. When it did and Lydia was contacted about selling it, Lydia said that it had come into her hands from Daniel, a collector who wished anonymity, and that she could make no promises about its authenticity. As Lydia had hoped, Stephen paid her $400 for the letter. Later Stephen discovered that the letter was not authentic, and handwriting analysis established that Lydia had written the letter.

In a jurisdiction that follows the common-law definition of forgery, Lydia has:
call: In a jurisdiction that follows the common-law definition of forgery, Lydia has:

choices.A: committed both forgery and false pretenses.
choices.B: committed forgery, because a writing that can induce a collector to pay money has apparent legal significance, and has committed false pretenses because she lied about the source of the document.
choices.C: not committed forgery, because the document had no apparent legal significance, but has committed false pretenses, since she misrepresented the source of the document.
choices.D: not committed forgery, because the document had no apparent legal significance, and has not committed false pretenses, since she made no representation as to authenticity of the document.

rightExplanation:
C is correct.

Gold Key: Common-law forgery needs more than a fake-looking writing and fraud intent. The writing must have apparent legal efficacy or be capable of founding legal liability. A private collectible devotional letter has market value, but that does not make it a legal instrument.

Gold Key: False pretenses is about obtaining title to property through a knowingly false material representation with intent to defraud. Lydia did not promise authenticity, but she did lie about the letter’s source and history. That source lie induced Stephen to transfer title to the $400.

Silver Key: Split the answer into two crime boxes. Do not let “fake signature” automatically become forgery. Do not let “no authenticity promise” erase a separate source/history lie.

c3.label: CUT A
c3.text: “Both crimes” over-includes forgery. Needs the forgery legal-efficacy Gold Key.

c3.label: CUT B
c3.text: Invents “collector value = legal significance.” Same forgery trap, cleaner mold.

c3.label: CUT D
c3.text: Correct on forgery, but not responsive to the false-pretenses fact. The answer talks authenticity; the stem gives a source/history lie.

c3.label: CLASH/CALL
c3.text: No final two-answer clash remains after anchor-assisted CUT. The answer is an anchor-assisted CUT-to-one.

studentScript: Split the crimes. Fake signature: check legal efficacy. No legal instrument, so no forgery. Money sale: check lie causing title transfer. Source lie caused payment, so false pretenses. Pick C.

A.signal: This answer correctly sees the money fraud but lets fake signature equal forgery without checking the writing threshold.
A.lawyer: Forgery fails because the private letter lacks apparent legal efficacy; false pretenses remains true.

B.signal: The answer invents a bridge from collector value to legal significance.
B.lawyer: A writing's ability to induce payment does not itself make the writing legally efficacious for common-law forgery.

C.signal: This answer keeps the two boxes separate and uses the source lie, not the authenticity disclaimer, for false pretenses.
C.lawyer: Common-law forgery fails on legal efficacy; false pretenses is satisfied by material misrepresentation causing title to money to pass.

D.signal: The answer answers the authenticity promise; the stem's live fraud fact is the source/history story.
D.lawyer: A source/provenance misrepresentation can support false pretenses even without an express authenticity warranty.

goldKeys.statement: Common-law forgery requires a false making or material alteration of a writing that, if genuine, would have apparent legal efficacy or found legal liability. A private collectible letter can be valuable without being a forgery object.
goldKeys.trigger: Fake private letter, keepsake, memorabilia, or collectible with no legal effect
goldKeys.authority: Moskal v. United States; Smith v. State; Cornell Wex forgery

goldKeys.statement: False pretenses is satisfied when a knowing material lie about a past or existing fact causes the victim to transfer title. A provenance/source lie can matter even when authenticity is disclaimed.
goldKeys.trigger: Seller says no authenticity promise but lies about source, ownership, or history
goldKeys.authority: Cornell Wex false pretenses; Morales-Alegria v. Gonzales

silverKeys.statement: When the choices combine two crimes, split them into boxes and resolve each box separately before selecting the combined answer.
silverKeys.trigger: Answer choices say both, first only, second only, or neither

remediation.title: Fake Document vs Fraud Sale
remediation.signal: Fake private letter plus money transfer
remediation.studentMove: Ask first whether the writing itself has legal effect; then ask whether a separate lie caused title to pass.
remediation.tinyRule: Forgery is about legal-efficacy writing; false pretenses is about title-transfer fraud.
remediation.trap: Letting the fake signature do all the work.
